courses.title: 100 Days of Code: The Complete Python Pro Bootcamp
courses.provider: Udemy / The App Brewery (Dr. Angela Yu)
courses.format: self-paced video bootcamp, 100 daily sections each ending in a project; levels: Beginner (Days 1-14), Intermediate (15-31), Intermediate+ (32-58), Advanced (59-81), Professional Portfolio (82-100)
courses.audience: absolute beginners through to aspiring professional developers
courses.notes: Udemy course page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so day titles were reconstructed from multiple student GitHub repos that mirror the Udemy section titles; these agree closely. Numbering follows the current (2024+) edition, which inserted 'Day 70: Git, GitHub and Version Control' and moved deployment to Day 71 (Render + gunicorn + PostgreSQL, replacing Heroku); as a result the data-science block is Days 72-81 (vs 71-80 in 2021-2023 editions) and the old 'Predict Earnings using Multivariable Regression' day appears dropped, with Days 99-100 being Space Race and Fatal Force (police deaths) analyses. Older editions differ by one day from Day 70 onward. Days 41-44 (HTML/CSS) were folded in from Angela Yu's web bootcamp in later editions. Days 82-100 are Professional Portfolio projects given only as briefs (no solutions/lectures), so their concepts are inferred from the brief and typical student implementations and are lower confidence; Day 98 is 'Automate Your Life' (open-ended). Day 13 has no main project. Exact sub-lesson topic wording is paraphrased from repos and memory of the course, not copied from Udemy. Some project names (e.g. Day 35 SMS vs Telegram rain alert after Twilio changes) vary by edition.

courses.title: Boot.dev Back-end Developer Path (Python + Go)
courses.format: self-paced interactive online track: 16 courses + 8 projects (6 guided, 2 portfolio), in-browser exercises plus local projects
courses.audience: beginners aiming for back-end developer roles
courses.notes: Course list and order taken from boot.dev/tracks/backend as fetched 2026-10-12 (24 items). Order differs from older versions of the path: Build an AI Agent now comes right after Functional Programming and before DSA; Static Site Generator follows DSA. Courses present in older path versions (e.g. Learn CI/CD, Kubernetes, earlier JavaScript/TypeScript courses) are NOT in the current listing, so no cicd/kubernetes/javascript concepts are included. Topics are the published chapter titles; individual lesson titles are not shown on public course pages, so concept mappings below chapter level are inferred from chapter descriptions and general knowledge of the courses (e.g. regex/unittest/enums in the SSG, match statement in Sum Types, sys.argv in BookBot, binary/bitwise in 'Computing'), and should be treated as moderately confident. The 'Learn Python for Beginners' slug is learn-python-beginners (marketed as Learn to Code in Python). The AI Agent project currently uses free models on OpenRouter via the OpenAI Python SDK (earlier versions used Google Gemini). The SQL course page does not name its engine (believed SQLite in-browser; uncertain). Portfolio projects (Personal Project 1, Capstone) list no public chapters. Python-language concept IDs are reused for analogous Go constructs only where noted via course_label (e.g. enums, modules_imports, pointers). Python-based modules are 1,3,5,6,7,8,9,10; Linux and Git are language-agnostic; Memory Management is C; most later courses are Go.

courses.title: Code in Place (Stanford)
courses.format: free online, 6 weeks of lessons (video lectures + worked examples + browser IDE) with weekly small-group live sections led by volunteer section leaders, followed by an optional final project; ~7 hrs/week
courses.audience: absolute beginners worldwide (no prior experience); covers roughly the first half of Stanford CS106A in Python
sources: https://codeinplace.stanford.edu/ (syllabus table embedded in the site's JS bundle: assets/default-CDCrfV2J.js; weekly titles also in assets/CourseRoutes-B09XBB48.js, retrieved 2026-10-12)
https://codeinplace.stanford.edu/cip5/certificate/3cnzhc (2025 certificate: Apr 21 - Jun 6 2025; Units: Karel the Robot, Console Programming, Graphics/Lists/Dictionaries)
https://github.com/mkrdip/codeinplace-2024 (CIP 2024 section leader materials: weekly section topics and section problems)
https://github.com/hulyak/code_in_place (CIP 2021 weekly outline, for edition comparison)
https://web.stanford.edu/class/archive/cs/cs106a/cs106a.1206/ (CS106A Spring 2020 lecture list, the source of CIP lesson titles)
courses.notes: Edition: the current official public syllabus (codeinplace.stanford.edu, used for the 2024/2025 runs; 2026 run starts Apr 2026) gives 6 weeks: W1 Control Flow with Karel (build: Welcome Karel), W2 The Art of Coding (Puzzle Karel), W3 Console Programs (Sandcastles), W4 Understanding Variables (Khansole Academy), W5 Graphics (Random Art), W6 Lists + Dictionaries (World's Hardest Game), then 'Beyond': Final Project. The in-app week labels differ slightly (W4 'Python Control Flow', W6 'Lists + Dicts'), and 2024 section-leader materials label W4 'Python Control Flow'. Week-level topics and the 'You Build' assignments are verified from the official site. Individual LESSON titles live behind login (Firestore) and could not be fetched; the per-lesson modules here are a reconstruction that splits each week into its lessons using the CS106A lecture titles CIP has historically reused (Intro to Karel, Control Flow, Decomposition, Intro to Python/Variables, Expressions, Control Flow Revisited, Functions Revisited/parameters, Graphics, Animation, Lists, Dictionaries) plus the 'Random' lesson referenced in the site's Khansole Academy materials. Exact lesson names/boundaries may differ; the 'Animation' lesson in W5 and the placement of parameters/return (W4 vs W5; a 2024 section placed it in W5 with graphics) are the least certain. Section problems listed in projects (e.g. Hospital Karel, Planetary Weight, High-Low, Heads Up) come from one 2024 section leader's repo and are marked '(section)'. Earlier editions differed: 2020/2021 were ~5 weeks + final project and included Images (SimpleImage), Text Processing, Files and Data Science; Images is NOT in the 2023+ syllabus, so no images module is included. No certificate grade; completion requires assignments in all three units (Karel, Console, Graphics) and attending sections.

courses.title: Codecademy Python: Learn Python 3 + Learn Intermediate Python 3
courses.format: self-paced interactive browser course; Learn Python 3 (13 modules, ~24 h, 14 lessons, 14 projects, 13 quizzes, 21 articles, 1 video) followed by Learn Intermediate Python 3 (9 modules, ~20 h, 11 lessons, 7 projects, 11 quizzes, 5 articles, 2 videos)
courses.audience: Learn Python 3: beginners with no prerequisites; Learn Intermediate Python 3: learners who finished Learn Python 3
courses.notes: Retrieved 2026-10-12 from the course pages' embedded syllabus data (module titles, content-item types and titles) and from each lesson page's exercise list. Learn Python 3 is described as teaching Python 3.13; both courses are marked Pro-only (paid plan) with certificates. Module titles are prefixed with the course name. topics list each content item with its type (Lesson/Quiz/Article/Video/Informational); parenthesised text summarises the lesson's exercise titles. Quizzes are named after their lesson and are not separately scored here. Projects named in older versions of the course or the CS path (e.g. 'Hurricane Analysis', 'Scrabble') are NOT in the current Learn Python 3 syllabus and were omitted; current named projects are listed per module. The Intermediate 'Unit Testing' module also contains the Exceptions lesson (exceptions/raising/custom exceptions are first taught there, not in Learn Python 3, except for the 'Errors in Python' debugging lesson). Specialized Collections covers sets plus the collections module; Resource Management covers context managers incl. contextlib. 'Namespaces' is mapped to the 'scope' concept. Concept mappings for articles, videos and projects are inferred from titles (not opened); depth ratings are judgement calls. Codecademy also offers split-out mini-courses (e.g. 'Learn Intermediate Python 3: Functions, Namespaces, and Scope') that repackage this content; they were not captured separately. New concept IDs: itertools_module, collections_module.

courses.title: CS50's Introduction to Programming with Python (CS50P)
courses.format: self-paced (OpenCourseWare / edX), 10 weeks (Week 0-9) of lectures + 9 problem sets + final project
courses.audience: beginners; no prior programming experience required
courses.notes: Edition: lectures/notes are the 2022 recording (CDN paths cdn.cs50.net/python/2022/x/; submit50 slugs cs50/problems/2022/python/...), still the current OCW edition as of retrieval; problem sets show a 2027-06-30 deadline and were updated in place (e.g. Bitcoin Price Index now uses the CoinCap v3 API with an API key). Weeks are numbered 0-9 as on the site; module 'order' follows that numbering, with the Final Project as order 10. Week 9 (Et Cetera) has no problem set. Topics are the h2/h3 headings of the official lecture notes (Summing Up headings omitted). Per-problem library mappings verified from problem pages for psets 4, 6, 7, 8; Guessing Game/Little Professor use random (from problem names/lecture, not individually verified). lambda (as sort key) appears in Lecture 6 body text, not a heading. Lecture 9 also mentions pyttsx3 and Sphinx (not modeled). Depth ratings are editorial judgments based on headings and problem-set emphasis. Lecture 8 decorators are taught via @property/@classmethod/@staticmethod, not writing custom decorators.

courses.title: Python Programming MOOC 2026
courses.provider: University of Helsinki (Department of Computer Science, MOOC Center)
courses.format: self-paced, 14 parts; Introduction to Programming (BSCS1001, parts 1-7, 5 ECTS) + Advanced Course in Programming (BSCS1002, parts 8-14, 5 ECTS); auto-graded TMC exercises, Zoom lectures, exams
courses.notes: Edition: 2026 (programming-26.mooc.fi, open until end of 2026); the 2025 edition (programming-25.mooc.fi) has an identical part/section structure. The site labels parts only by number ('Part 1'...'Part 14'); module titles here are composed from the official section titles, which are listed verbatim in `topics`. Section titles and exercise names were taken from the course's public source repo (rage/programming-26). `projects` lists a selection of notable/multi-part exercises, not every exercise (each part has ~15-40 exercises). Part 14 is a pygame game project (a Sokoban-style 'robot and boxes' worked example, then a peer-reviewed game of the student's own). Part 1-3 exercises run in an in-browser editor; VS Code + TMC plugin are introduced in part 4. Concept depth is a judgement from section content/exercise counts. 'polymorphism' is only implicit (method overriding in part 10), not named as such; 'math_module' is used in part 1 (sqrt for quadratic equation) but modules are formally taught in part 7. Not covered: sets as a topic, enumerate/zip, unit testing (tests are run by TMC but not taught), dataclasses, decorators beyond @property/@classmethod. New concept IDs: conditional_expressions, event_driven_programming.

courses.title: 6.100L Introduction to CS and Programming using Python
courses.format: full-semester lecture course, 26 lectures (2x/week), 6 problem sets (PS0 ungraded + PS1–PS5), finger exercises, microquizzes
courses.audience: students with little or no programming experience; no prerequisites; Python 3
courses.notes: Edition: OCW Fall 2022 (the only OCW edition of 6.100L found). 6.100L is the slower full-semester version of 6.100A (formerly 6.0001); textbook Guttag, Introduction to Computation and Programming Using Python, 3rd ed. A Fall 2025 introcomp.mit.edu site exists (described as 'the old 6.100L') but is behind MIT login, so not used; the MIT catalog has since reorganized intro CS (6.100A/6.100B/6.1000). Lecture titles are verbatim from 'Materials by Lecture'; module topics are taken from the OCW Calendar topic column (lecture slides were not individually parsed), so per-lecture concept lists are inferred from those titles/topics and are approximate. Problem sets are attached to the lecture at which they were released per the calendar (PS0 L1, PS1 L2, PS2 L9, PS3 L12, PS4 L16, PS5 L20); PS concepts come from the PS PDFs (PS1 compound interest incl. bisection search; PS2 Hangman; PS3 Document Distance with dictionaries/TF-IDF; PS4 recursion on trees + Caesar/one-time-pad cipher with Message class hierarchy; PS5 Using Libraries: PIL colorblindness filters and image steganography). Lecture 25 'Plotting' assumed to use matplotlib (calendar says 'visualization library'). Concepts 'random_module' and 'simulation_monte_carlo' in L26 inferred from 'Simulations'. PS concepts taught in later lectures (e.g. bisection in PS1 Part C, classes/inheritance in PS4 Parts B–C) are attached to the lecture that teaches them rather than the release lecture. Concept first_module reflects first appearance including problem-set concepts (e.g. file_io via Hangman word loading at L9).

courses.title: Python for Everybody (PY4E): Exploring Data in Python 3
courses.provider: University of Michigan (Dr. Charles Severance); also Coursera Python for Everybody Specialization
courses.format: self-paced; 17 py4e.com lessons (install + 16 textbook chapters) mapped onto a 5-course Coursera specialization
courses.notes: Modules = py4e.com lessons (install + book chapters 1-16; ch14 OOP is taught after ch13 in Course 4). Coursera mapping recorded as the first entry of each module's topics: C1 Programming for Everybody = install + ch1-5; C2 Python Data Structures = ch6-10; C3 Using Python to Access Web Data = ch11-13; C4 Using Databases with Python = ch14-15; C5 Capstone (Retrieving, Processing, and Visualizing Data with Python) = ch16 visualization worked examples plus peer-graded open-ended projects. The C1-C4 chapter mapping comes from course descriptions via mirror sites (Coursera pages were not fetched directly); Coursera also repeats an install week in later courses. Topics are the html3 book section headings verbatim (Glossary/Exercises omitted), plus 'Lecture:' items taken from py4e.com lesson video titles. Projects = autograder/peer-graded assignments listed on py4e.com lesson pages (quizzes omitted); ch14 lists no autograder; ch16 projects are worked examples rather than graded assignments, and Capstone peer-graded assignment names were not verified. Exercise 7.1 is a worked exercise on the lesson page; only 7.2 is listed as an autograder there (both included). The current online book edition's ch13 has generic 'Application Programming Interfaces' and 'Security and API usage' sections (older editions covered Google geocoding and the Twitter API); the GeoJSON/geocoding API assignment is on py4e.com's own py4e-data proxy. lesson slug 'servces' is a typo on py4e.com, kept as-is in the URL.
